newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Better days seen ahead on shrinking SKorea deficit.
newsitem.headline: Better days seen ahead on shrinking SKorea deficit.

text.p: A significant narrowing of South Korea's current account deficit in June, coupled with the country's first monthly trade surplus since December 1995, were signs of better days ahead, analysts said on Monday.
The central Bank of Korea said on Monday the current account deficit had shrunk to $361.4 million in June from a $1.31 billion shortfall a year ago.
"A gradual improvement in the current account deficit would not be a surprise for the second half," said Lee Won-il, head of research at KEB Smith Barney Securities.
He said imports would slow in the second half as Korean companies traditionally secure necessary raw materials in the first six months.
Rhee Namuh, head of research at Dongbang Peregrine Securities, said: "The figures for the second half should be better than the first half because of the weak domestic economy."
Rhee said very slow private consumption and capital investment expected for the second half would drag imports.
The deficit totalled $10.3 billion for the first half of this year, against $9.82 billion a year before, the bank said.

The bank attributed the decline in the current account deficit in June to strong growth in heavy industrial and chemical exports, which led to a trade surplus of $264.6 million, compared to a deficit of $655.1 million a year ago.
Free-on-board exports rose 11.6 percent year-on-year, while imports increased 2.9 percent.
"South Korea's exports have generally been strong in June and December as companies attempt to improve their half- and full-year financial statements," said Lee of KEB Smith Barney.
Customs-cleared exports of heavy industrial and chemical goods rose 8.9 percent in June to $8.33 billion, while those of light industrial products gained 6.1 percent to $3.14 billion, the bank said.
On the other hand, customs-cleared imports of raw materials rose 4.1 percent to $6.12 billion in June, while imports of food and consumer goods dropped 7.7 percent to $1.33 billion.
The bank said increases in overseas travel and transportation expenses were largely responsible for a $600.5 million invisible trade deficit in June and $3.90 billion in the first half.
"The current account deficit in the second half is expected to be smaller than that of the first half," said Kim In-seob, an economist at the central bank.
An expected rise in international prices of South Korea's major export items and growing demand from overseas could make that possible, he said.
"A recovery in the second half will put the current account deficit for the whole year at around $16.5 billion, lower than the official projection of $17 billion."
The Bank of Korea had earlier forecast this year's current account deficit at $17 billion, compared with a $23.72 billion shortfall in 1996.
